endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Rather than building entirely new infrastructure, much of this can be embedded into what HDOs already have: non-retaliation language can be updated to reference AI specifically within existing HR policies, AI-related reporting categories can be added to current compliance hotline intake forms, and whistleblower protections can be incorporated into the AI modules of onboarding and annual training programs.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether offering multiple accessible channels for AI feedback and incident reporting increases reports from people with disabilities or access barriers, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on a single framework endorsement from CHAI, which uses permissive language ("may").

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single endorsement is a governance playbook, which reflects expert judgment and does not substitute for comparative data on reporting rates or harm detection.

The CHAI playbook proposes embedding AI reporting in existing structures, such as adding AI categories to compliance hotline intake forms and updating non-retaliation language in HR policies. This approach suggests the added cost may be modest, but no supplied study measures cost, staffing needs, or whether added channels receive any use.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI incident reporting volume, reporter characteristics, and time to harm detection before and after health systems add accessible channels such as phone, text, sign language video, screen-reader-compatible web forms, and multilingual options. Such studies should also establish whether people with disabilities or access barriers currently underreport AI problems relative to other patients.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, low-literacy, or disability populations, because no study was supplied at all. Health systems adopting this practice therefore have no evidence on which channels reach these groups and should track channel use by patient population to generate that evidence locally.
